title: The eyes weep
hook: when his small son Ibrahim died, the Prophet wept: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves (Sahih al-Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ground that remembers and your line, ground that remembers. Which small good did you do? The week's last day brings tears, and a father holding his son. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

The house of a blacksmith named Abu Saif. His wife is nursing a little boy named Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. A companion named Anas remembers going there with the Prophet, who took the child, kissed him and breathed in his smell, the way parents do. Some time later they came again. This time Ibrahim was dying. And Anas remembers what happened next: the Prophet's eyes began to fill with tears.
screen: `A BLACKSMITH'S HOUSE.` → `A FATHER KISSES HIS SON.` → `THE SECOND VISIT.`

segments.voice: First, a small son. The report in Sahih al-Bukhari doesn't start with doctrine. It starts with a father holding a child close enough to breathe him in. Before anything is said about death, we're shown love. Second, even you? A companion named Abdur Rahman ibn Awf is standing there, and he's surprised. He says something like: you too, O Messenger of God? As if a prophet should be above tears. Third, this is mercy. The Prophet answers him: this is mercy. The tears aren't a lapse in faith. In this report they are a sign of the mercy God puts in human hearts. Fourth, eyes, heart and tongue. Then the Prophet says the line the story is remembered for: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And then, to the child: O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting. Three parts of a person, each given its job. The eyes are allowed to weep. The heart is allowed to grieve. The tongue is asked to hold to what pleases God, no cursing fate, no wild words. For Muslims, patience in grief limits what is said, not whether tears fall. Look back over the week. Paul taunting death. Francis calling it sister. The old art, against clinging, letting go. Names in a book, and purgatory. Every soul tasting death, a dharra of good. And now a father crying over his boy, and calling it mercy. The eyes weep.
screen: `A FATHER HOLDS HIS SON.` · `"EVEN YOU?"` · `TEARS ARE MERCY.` · `EYES WEEP, HEART GRIEVES, TONGUE HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE EYES WEEP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind a loss, recent or old, large or small. You don't need to go looking for pain; just let whatever is near come close. If tears come, let them come. Nobody needs to see them, and there's nothing to fix. If they don't come, that's fine too. Just let the heart feel what it feels, and keep the words gentle, even the ones in your own head. If you pray, you can bring the grief to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ibrahim, the small son of the Prophet Muhammad, whose death made the Prophet's eyes fill with tears he called mercy. Today's word.
Your line: this is mercy. Today, if you're with someone who cries, don't hurry them out of it. Tears can be mercy. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims point to this hadith to show that weeping over the dead is permitted and merciful, while wailing and words of protest against God's decree are discouraged; mourners are encouraged to say the Quran's words that we belong to God and to Him we are returning (2:156).

fork.setup: you're the Prophet, at your dying son's side. a companion asks why you, of all people, are weeping. what do you say?
fork.reveal: he answers, this is mercy, and adds: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves.

original.note: Arabic, from the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: truly, the eye weeps.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Islam, people of faith shouldn't cry at a death.
what it means: the Prophet wept for his son and called the tears mercy.
what a scholar hears: the hadith gives eyes, heart and tongue each a role; restraint falls on speech, not on tears.
recall: goes out on the road to meet Jesus

notes: Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 paraphrased throughout: Abu Saif the blacksmith, husband of Ibrahim's wet nurse; kissing and smelling the child; the second visit; Abdur Rahman ibn Awf's question; 'this is mercy'; 'the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord; O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting'. Confirm the number and wording.
'His wife is nursing a little boy' (wet nurse): confirm.
The index hook says 'infant'; the script says 'little boy' / 'small son' to avoid an age claim.
